bugs: Job never checks that its rows are still claimed (app/Jobs/PushStockAllocations.php:32-35). SQS delivers at least once, so a redelivered or duplicate message pushes rows that are already synced again. Probe: running dispatchSync twice sent 2 HTTP requests.

routes/console.php:11 calls withoutOverlapping() with the default 1440-minute mutex expiry. If a scheduler container dies mid-run (deploy, OOM), stock:dispatch-sync is blocked on all three servers for 24 hours.
synced_at uses second precision. An edit in the same second after the rows are read gives updated_at == synced_at, so the change is never re-sent (probe confirmed; the other two have the same issue).

failed() clears sync_started_at on every id without checking whose claim it is. A stale job that fails after its rows were re-claimed releases the newer claim and causes a duplicate dispatch (probe confirmed). retryUntil makes this rare.

bugs: Job retry lifetime is not tied to the 15-minute claim TTL. #[Tries(10)] combined with 429 releases of up to 600s and backoff up to 300s lets a job keep retrying well past 15 minutes. The dispatcher then re-claims the rows and dispatches a second job. The old job still passes whereNotNull('sync_started_at') and pushes duplicates, and its later failed() clears the new claim, which triggers yet another dispatch (probe confirmed the claim stomping). This is exactly the rate-limited scenario the task describes.
synced_at uses second precision, so a same-second edit during the request is lost (probe confirmed; shared by all three).
app/Providers/AppServiceProvider.php:23 Schedule::useCache('redis') hard-codes the store, so local and dev environments need Redis even when CACHE_STORE is set differently.
antipatterns: app/Jobs/PushStockAllocations.php:16 Tries/Backoff chosen with no relation to StockAllocation::CLAIM_TIMEOUT_MINUTES
app/Console/Commands/DispatchStockSync.php:20-26 claims via chunkById with a separate update and no transaction or row lock, so it relies entirely on onOneServer
app/Jobs/PushStockAllocations.php:29 inline \DateTimeInterface in the factory, and the job does not skip disabled rows
tests/Feature/StockAllocationTest.php:147-156 the 'edit made after the rows were read' test edits after the job finishes, so it would pass even if synced_at were taken after the request

Caps the Retry-After delay and falls back to 60s; config-driven storefront URL

v.rationale:
I ran `php artisan test` on all three (17, 20 and 16 tests, all passing), read every added or changed file, and ran six throwaway probes on each, then deleted them. All three share two edge bugs. First, a same-second edit during the HTTP request is lost because timestamps have second precision. Second, failed() clears claims without checking ownership. The ranking comes down to how each one ties queue retries to the 15-minute claim TTL, and whether a job survives SQS delivering it more than once.

impl-2 gets both right. It uses tries=0 with retryUntil(10 min) below the TTL, plus a claim guard in handle(), so a duplicate delivery sends nothing. It also claims under a transaction with lockForUpdate, sets withoutOverlapping(10), and has the best in-flight-edit test. Its flaws are idiom-level: an unused import, the old scope syntax, a hard-coded 10 instead of a value derived from the TTL, and redundant fillable/model settings.

impl-1 is the most idiomatic and derives retryUntil from the TTL. However, its job doesn't check the claim, so SQS redelivery causes duplicate pushes (probe: 2 requests). Its withoutOverlapping() also keeps the default 24-hour mutex, which can stop syncing on all servers after a crash.

impl-3 has the cleanest modern syntax, but nothing bounds its retry lifetime: 10 tries with 429 delays of up to 600s. Under the 429 storms the task describes, jobs outlive the claim. That leads to re-claims, duplicate pushes, and old jobs' failed() releasing newer claims. It also hard-codes Schedule::useCache('redis') and has a weaker in-flight-edit test. That design flaw in the task's focus area puts it last.
